findings.description: The RDS instance sets publicly_accessible = true, giving it a public IP and exposing the MySQL endpoint to the internet rather than keeping it private within the VPC.
storage_encrypted = false means the RDS database volume and its snapshots are not encrypted at rest, exposing catalog data if storage media or snapshots are accessed.

The master password is supplied via var.password and passed directly into the resource, storing the plaintext credential in Terraform state and likely in variable files; the hardcoded username 'admin' is also a predictable default that aids brute forcing.
iam_database_authentication_enabled is not set, so the database relies solely on a static master password for authentication instead of short-lived IAM credentials.

The database password (var.password) and username are interpolated into the instance user_data script, which is stored unencrypted in EC2 metadata and Terraform state and is readable by anyone who can reach the instance metadata service.

No metadata_options block requiring http_tokens = "required" is set, so IMDSv1 remains enabled; combined with a PHP web app this allows SSRF to steal the instance profile credentials granting s3:*, ec2:*, and rds:*.
No root_block_device with encrypted = true is specified, so the instance's root volume (which also contains the plaintext dbinfo.inc credentials file) is likely unencrypted at rest.
The instance role grants s3:*, ec2:*, and rds:* on Resource "*", violating least privilege; compromise of the web server yields near-full control of storage, compute, and databases in the account.
The database security group allows all outbound traffic on all protocols to 0.0.0.0/0, enabling data exfiltration or C2 callbacks from a compromised database host.
MySQL port 3306 is open to the entire VPC CIDR rather than restricted to the application server's security group, allowing any instance in the VPC to attempt database access.
